title: Solidity Programming for Beginners
tagline: Read, reason about and design Solidity contracts: types, functions, data, ETH, inheritance and a full project
summary: A beginner's course in Solidity built around complete, compiled example contracts: types and structure, control flow and modifiers, mappings, arrays and structs, receiving and sending ETH safely, events and custom errors, inheritance and OpenZeppelin, and a full Crowdfund project with a test suite. You read and reason about code in the course labs, and run the examples yourself in the free Remix editor.

modules.title: Setting up and the basics
modules.summary: Your first environment, the structure of a Solidity file, the basic types and the difference between constants, immutables and state variables.
modules.outcome: You can open Remix, read the structure of a contract and choose the right type for a piece of data.
modules.intro: Solidity looks like a blend of JavaScript and C, with a few concepts that exist only because the code runs on a blockchain. This module gets you set up and builds the vocabulary you need to read any contract.

topics.title: Your workspace: Remix
topics.html:
You do not need to install anything to start. Remix is a free development environment that runs in your web browser (remix.ethereum.org). It has an editor, a compiler, a built-in test blockchain with fake accounts and ETH, and a panel for calling your contracts.

The parts of Remix you will use
PanelWhat it is for
File explorerCreate and edit .sol files
Solidity compilerPick the compiler version and compile; errors appear with line numbers
Deploy and runChoose an environment, deploy a contract and call its functions
TerminalShows transactions, logs, gas and error messages
Tip

Always check the compiler version matches your pragma. A mismatch is a very common first error.

Check what you just learned

1. What does the built-in Remix environment give you?
  • A test blockchain with fake accounts and ETH (correct)
  • Real ETH
  • A bank account
  • A hardware wallet

Safe practice.

Check what you just learned

1. The first thing to check when a compile fails with a version message is:
  • The wallet
  • The pragma and the compiler version (correct)
  • The fee
  • The block

They must be compatible.
keyPoints: Remix is a free browser tool with an editor, compiler and test chain.
The loop is edit, compile, deploy, call, repeat.

topics.title: The structure of a contract
topics.html:
Parts of the file
LineWhat it does
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MITStates the licence of the code
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;Allowed compiler versions
contract Basics { ... }The container for state and functions
constantA value fixed when you write the code; costs no storage
immutableA value set once in the constructor and fixed afterwards; cheap to read
publicCreates a free getter for the variable
constructorRuns once, at deployment

Comments start with // or sit between /* and */. Statements end with a semicolon. Blocks use curly braces. Names are case-sensitive, and by convention contracts are in PascalCase and variables in camelCase.

Check what you just learned

1. When does a constructor run?
  • Every call
  • Every block
  • Once, at deployment (correct)
  • Only when ETH arrives

It sets up initial state.

Check what you just learned

1. An immutable variable is set:
  • In memory
  • Every call
  • By users
  • In the constructor, then fixed (correct)

It cannot change afterwards.
keyPoints: A file has a licence line, a pragma and contracts.
constant and immutable values save gas compared with storage.

topics.title: Types and global variables
topics.html:
Value types
TypeHoldsExample
uint8 ... uint256Unsigned whole numbers of a given sizeuint256 balance = 100;
int8 ... int256Signed whole numbersint256 change = -5;
booltrue or falsebool open = true;
addressA 20-byte account addressaddress owner;
address payableAn address that can receive ETH via transfer-style callsaddress payable seller;
bytes1 ... bytes32Fixed-size raw bytesbytes32 tag;
enumA named list of optionsenum Status { Open, Closed }
Reference types
TypeHoldsWhere it lives
stringTextStorage, memory or calldata
bytesA dynamic byte arrayStorage, memory or calldata
arraysLists of one typeStorage, memory or calldata
structA group of named fieldsStorage, memory or calldata
mappingA lookup tableStorage only
Global variables you will use constantly
NameMeaning
msg.senderThe address that called the current function
msg.valueThe wei sent with the call
block.timestampThe time of the current block, in seconds
block.numberThe current block number
address(this)This contract's own address
address(this).balanceThis contract's ETH balance in wei

How big can an integer be?

Change the number of bits to see how many values a uint of that size can hold.

Adjust Bits and see Largest value change.

Watch out

Solidity has no decimals. To handle fractions you use whole numbers with an agreed scale: for example, amounts in wei (10^-18 ETH) or percentages in basis points.

Check what you just learned

1. address(this).balance is:
  • This contract's ETH balance in wei (correct)
  • The caller's balance
  • The block number
  • The gas price

The contract's own holdings.

Key terms: flip and sort

Remix
A browser-based IDE for Solidity
pragma
Sets the compiler version range
constant
A value fixed in the code
immutable
A value fixed at deployment
address
A 20-byte account identifier
wei
The smallest unit of ETH
keyPoints: Choose the smallest sensible type; Solidity has no decimals.
msg.sender, msg.value and block.timestamp are the most-used globals.

modules.title: Control flow and functions
modules.summary: Conditions, loops, functions, modifiers and the three ways to stop a transaction.
modules.outcome: You can write functions with the right visibility and mutability, use modifiers for access control and choose between require, revert and assert.
modules.intro: Real contracts are built from small functions with clear rules about who may call them and when they must fail. This module teaches the control structures and the safety tools that go with them.

topics.title: Conditions and loops
topics.html:
Conditions use if, else if and else. Loops use for and while, but remember that every iteration costs gas, so loops over data that can grow without limit are dangerous: one day the loop costs more than a block can hold, and the function becomes impossible to call.

Safe and unsafe loop habits
SafeUnsafe
Loop a small, fixed number of timesLoop over every user in an array that anyone can add to
Let users act on their own item (pull)Pay everyone in one transaction (push)
Cap the input with requireTrust the input size
Process in batches across several transactionsProcess everything at once

Check what you just learned

1. Why is looping over a growing array risky?
  • It is slow only on test networks
  • Gas can exceed the block limit, making the function unusable (correct)
  • Loops are not allowed
  • It uses memory

Unbounded work is a denial-of-service risk.

The sum loop

The function sumTo(n) adds 1 to n. Change n to see the result and a rough gas figure (a teaching estimate of about 100 gas per iteration).

Adjust n and see sumTo(n), Rough extra gas change.

Check what you just learned

1. A safe design usually lets each user:
  • Pay everyone
  • Loop over all users
  • Pull their own payment (correct)
  • Wait for the owner

Pull over push.
keyPoints: if/else and for/while work as in other languages.
Avoid loops whose cost grows without limit.

topics.title: Functions, visibility and mutability
topics.html:
Visibility
KeywordCallable from
externalOutside only
publicOutside and inside
internalThis contract and children
privateThis contract only
State mutability
KeywordMeaningCosts gas when called from outside?
(none)May read and write stateYes, in a transaction
viewReads state, does not write itNo
pureNeither reads nor writes stateNo
payableMay receive ETHYes

A function signature has the shape: function name(type argument, ...) visibility mutability returns (type). Return values can be named. Functions can return more than one value.

Worked example

Reading a signature

function setValue(uint256 newValue) external onlyOwner whenNotPaused

  1. external: callable from outside the contract.
  2. uint256 newValue: one input.
  3. onlyOwner and whenNotPaused: two modifiers that run checks first.
  4. No view or pure, so it changes state and needs a transaction.

Answer. Signatures tell you who can call, what it takes and what it can do.

Check what you just learned

1. A function marked pure may:
  • Read storage
  • Emit events
  • Send ETH
  • Use only its arguments and local variables (correct)

No state, no chain data.

Check what you just learned

1. internal visibility means:
  • This contract and its children only (correct)
  • Anyone can call
  • Only outside
  • Nobody

Not exposed externally.
keyPoints: Visibility says who can call; mutability says what it can do.
view and pure functions are free to call from outside.

topics.title: Modifiers and errors
topics.html:
A modifier is a reusable check. The underscore _ marks where the function body runs. Stacking modifiers keeps functions short: onlyOwner whenNotPaused says everything about who and when.

Ways to fail
ToolUse it forNotes
require(cond, "message")Validating inputs and conditionsReadable messages, slightly more gas
revert CustomError()Cheap, specific failuresDefine errors with error Name();
assert(cond)Invariants that must never be falseA failure means a bug in your code

Check what you just learned

1. What does the underscore in a modifier mean?
  • End of file
  • The function body runs here (correct)
  • A comment
  • A private variable

The body is inserted at that point.

Common mistakes

  • Putting the whole access check into every function instead of a modifier.
  • Using assert for user input, which signals a bug instead of a bad request.
  • Forgetting that a revert undoes every change made in the transaction.

Check what you just learned

1. A revert:
  • Keeps partial changes
  • Mines a block
  • Undoes all changes in the transaction (correct)
  • Pays a bonus

Atomic failure.

Key terms: flip and sort

Visibility
Who may call a function
Mutability
Whether a function may change state
Modifier
A reusable pre-check
revert
Undo the transaction
assert
Check an invariant
Custom error
A named, cheap error type
keyPoints: Modifiers reuse checks; the underscore marks where the body runs.
Use require for input, custom errors for cheap failures and assert for invariants.

modules.title: Data structures
modules.summary: Mappings, arrays, structs and enums, and how to use them well.
modules.outcome: You can model real data with structs and mappings, know why mappings cannot be listed and use arrays safely.
modules.intro: Good contracts model their data carefully. Mappings give instant lookups, arrays give ordered lists, structs group related fields and enums name the stages of a process. Choosing among them well is a large part of writing efficient and safe code.

topics.title: A registry: structs, mappings and enums
topics.html:
What each piece does
PiecePurpose
enum Status { Pending, Active, Closed }Names the stages; internally just numbers 0, 1, 2
struct Student { name; grade; status }Groups the fields of one record
mapping(address => Student) public studentsLooks up a student by address in constant cost
address[] public idsKeeps a list of registered addresses so a front end can enumerate them
bytes(name).length == 0A way to check whether a string is empty or a mapping entry is unused
calldataA cheap read-only location for external inputs

Notice the three require lines. They check the name, the range of the grade and that the sender has not already enrolled. Validating early means the rest of the function can assume the input is good.

Check what you just learned

1. Why does the Registry keep an ids array as well as the mapping?
  • It is required
  • Arrays are cheaper
  • Mappings are slow
  • Mappings cannot be looped over or listed (correct)

A mapping has no list of its keys.

Check what you just learned

1. An enum is stored as:
  • A small number (correct)
  • Text
  • An address
  • A struct

Names for 0, 1, 2 and so on.
keyPoints: Structs group fields; mappings look up by key; arrays keep lists.
Mappings cannot be listed, so keep an array of keys when you need to.

topics.title: Storage, memory and calldata in practice
topics.html:
For reference types such as arrays, strings and structs, you must say where they live. This matters for both correctness and cost.

Rules of thumb
LocationUse whenRemember
storageReferring to persistent state, or changing itA storage pointer changes the original
memoryBuilding or changing temporary data inside a functionA memory copy does not change storage
calldataReading external function inputs without copyingRead-only and cheapest
Worked example

A common surprise

A function copies a struct from storage into memory and changes it.

  1. Student memory s = students[addr];
  2. s.grade = 12;
  3. The change affects only the memory copy, and storage is unchanged.
  4. To change the stored value use Student storage s = students[addr]; or write students[addr].grade = 12;

Answer. Copies change nothing in storage.

Habits

  1. Use calldata for external inputs you only read.
  2. Use storage pointers to modify state without copying.
  3. Avoid copying large arrays from storage to memory.
  4. Use delete to clear a value and get a gas refund.

Check what you just learned

1. You copy a struct from storage to memory and edit it. What happens to the stored struct?
  • It changes too
  • It stays unchanged (correct)
  • It is deleted
  • It becomes calldata

Memory is a separate copy.

Check what you just learned

1. To modify stored data without copying, use a:
  • memory variable
  • calldata variable
  • storage pointer (correct)
  • pure function

It refers to the original.
keyPoints: storage persists, memory is temporary, calldata is read-only input.
Editing a memory copy does not change storage.

topics.title: Choosing and using arrays safely
topics.html:
Choosing a structure
NeedUse
Fast lookup by keymapping
Ordered list that you must loop over (small)array
A record with several fieldsstruct
A fixed set of stagesenum
Both lookup and listingmapping plus an array of keys

The cost of looping

Change the number of items to see how a loop's gas grows linearly while a mapping lookup stays flat. A teaching estimate: 2,100 gas per first read of a storage slot.

Adjust Items in the array and see Gas to loop over all, Gas for one mapping lookup, Fits in a 30 million gas block? change.

Common mistakes

  • Removing array items by shifting every later item.
  • Letting anyone push to an array that you later loop over.
  • Using an array when a mapping would do.
Tip

A useful trick to remove an item cheaply: move the last item into the gap and pop the array. It changes the order, which is fine when order does not matter.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is the cheapest way to check if an address has voted?
  • Loop over an array of voters
  • An event
  • A string
  • A mapping from address to bool (correct)

Constant-cost lookup.

Check what you just learned

1. To remove an array item cheaply when order does not matter:
  • Swap in the last item and pop (correct)
  • Shift all items
  • Delete the whole array
  • Use a string

Constant cost.

Key terms: flip and sort

struct
A custom record type
mapping
A key to value lookup table
enum
A named set of options
calldata
Read-only external input
memory
Temporary data
storage
Persistent data
keyPoints: Use mappings for lookups and arrays for short, ordered lists.
Never loop over data that outsiders can grow without limit.

modules.title: Holding ETH, events and errors
modules.summary: Receiving and sending ETH safely, events for apps, and custom errors.
modules.outcome: You can write a contract that accepts and pays out ETH using safe patterns, and emit events that apps can follow.
modules.intro: Most useful contracts handle money. Money handling is where small mistakes become expensive, so this module goes slowly: how ETH arrives, how it leaves, and how to tell the outside world what happened.

topics.title: Receiving ETH
topics.html:
Ways a contract can receive ETH
MechanismWhen it runs
A payable function such as deposit()When the function is called with ETH
receive() external payableWhen ETH is sent with empty data (a plain transfer)
fallback() external payableWhen ETH or data arrives that matches no function and there is no receive
A constructor marked payableOnly at deployment

A contract with none of these rejects incoming ETH. A contract can also be forced to receive ETH by another contract that self-destructs or by a block producer's reward, so you should never rely on address(this).balance being exactly what your own records say.

Check what you just learned

1. Which function handles a plain ETH transfer with empty data?
  • fallback only
  • receive (correct)
  • constructor
  • withdraw

That is what receive is for.

Watch out

Tracking your own balances in a mapping, rather than trusting address(this).balance, avoids a class of accounting bugs.

Check what you just learned

1. A contract with no receive, fallback or payable function:
  • Accepts any ETH
  • Burns the ETH
  • Rejects ETH sent to it (correct)
  • Refunds later

The call reverts.
keyPoints: receive handles plain transfers; payable functions handle calls with ETH.
Track balances in your own state.

topics.title: Sending ETH safely
topics.html:
Three ways to send ETH
MethodGas forwardedNotes
recipient.transfer(amount)2,300 (fixed)Older; can fail when the recipient needs more gas; no longer recommended
recipient.send(amount)2,300Returns a bool; must be checked
recipient.call{value: amount}("")All availableRecommended today; returns a bool you must check; requires reentrancy care

The Vault's withdraw follows this order exactly. Because the balance is reduced before the external call, a recipient that calls back finds nothing left to take. The result of call is checked, so a failed payment undoes the whole transaction instead of silently losing track of the funds.

Common mistakes

  • Sending before updating balances.
  • Ignoring the boolean result of call or send.
  • Sending ETH to many addresses in one loop, so one failing recipient blocks everyone.

Check what you just learned

1. Which method is generally recommended for sending ETH today?
  • transfer
  • send
  • selfdestruct
  • call with value, checking the result (correct)

It forwards enough gas and returns a status.

Check what you just learned

1. The safe order for a withdrawal is:
  • Update, then send (correct)
  • Send, then update
  • Never update
  • Emit first

Effects before interactions.
keyPoints: Use call with value, check the result and update state first.
Prefer pull payments over looping pushes.

topics.title: Events and custom errors
topics.html:
Events are the contract's public log. Apps and explorers read them to show activity and to rebuild history cheaply, because storing history in variables is expensive. Up to three event parameters can be marked indexed, which makes them searchable by filters.

Designing events
PrincipleExample
Emit one for every important state changeDeposited, Withdrawn, OwnerChanged
Index the things people search byaddress indexed user
Include the data an app needs to display the changeamount, new value
Name them in the past tensePaused, not Pause
Custom errors versus strings
require with stringrevert CustomError()
Readability for usersMessage shown directlyWallets and explorers decode the name using the ABI
GasStores the text in the bytecode and returns itCheaper
Extra dataNoCan carry arguments, such as error Insufficient(uint256 have, uint256 need)

Check what you just learned

1. What does marking an event parameter indexed allow?
  • Hiding it
  • Searching and filtering logs by it (correct)
  • Making it cheaper to store
  • Changing its type

Filters can match it.

Tip

A good event list doubles as documentation: reading the events tells you what the contract is for.

Check what you just learned

1. Event names are conventionally:
  • Future tense
  • Numbers
  • Past tense (correct)
  • Random

They describe what happened.

Key terms: flip and sort

receive
Function for plain ETH transfers
fallback
Function for unmatched calls
call
Low-level call that can carry value
Pull payment
Recipients withdraw themselves
Indexed
Searchable event parameter
Custom error
A named, cheap error
keyPoints: Events are cheap logs; index what people search by.
Custom errors are cheaper and can carry data.

modules.title: Inheritance, interfaces and libraries
modules.summary: Reusing code safely: inheritance, interfaces, libraries and trusted building blocks such as OpenZeppelin.
modules.outcome: You can extend a base contract, program to an interface and use audited building blocks instead of writing everything yourself.
modules.intro: Professional contracts are mostly assembled from reviewed building blocks, with only the unique part written fresh. This module shows how Solidity supports reuse and how to use well-tested libraries instead of reinventing them.

topics.title: Inheritance and interfaces
topics.html:
What is going on
PieceMeaning
interface IGreeterDeclares what a greeter must offer: only function signatures
contract BaseA parent with an owner and an onlyOwner modifier
contract Greeter is Base, IGreeterInherits from both: gets the owner and modifier, and promises to implement greet()
overrideNeeded when implementing an interface function or replacing a parent function
onlyOwner on setGreetingUses the inherited modifier

An interface defines what other contracts can call without exposing the code. A contract that knows only the interface of another can talk to it at any address, which is how wallets, exchanges and tokens interact across projects.

Rules

  • A contract can inherit from several parents, with the order mattering.
  • Interface functions are all external and have no bodies.
  • Mark parent functions virtual if children may override them.
  • Keep inheritance shallow: deep hierarchies are hard to read and audit.

Check what you just learned

1. Why use an interface?
  • To make code run faster
  • To pay fees
  • To store data
  • So contracts can talk to each other without knowing the code (correct)

It defines a shared shape.

Check what you just learned

1. The keyword that marks implementing an interface function is:
  • override (correct)
  • is
  • virtual
  • abstract

Explicit and required.
keyPoints: Inheritance reuses parent state and functions; interfaces define shape only.
Keep hierarchies shallow.

topics.title: Libraries and OpenZeppelin
topics.html:
A library is reusable code without its own storage. Standard building blocks for tokens, access control and security are published as open-source libraries, and the most widely used is OpenZeppelin Contracts, which has been audited and used in thousands of projects. Reusing it is almost always safer than writing your own.

What OpenZeppelin gives you
ModuleProvides
OwnableA single owner and an onlyOwner modifier
AccessControlRoles such as admin and minter
ReentrancyGuardA lock to stop reentrancy
PausableAn emergency stop
ERC20, ERC721, ERC1155Standard tokens
SafeERC20, Math, AddressHelper libraries
Watch out

Library versions change their APIs. For example, version 5 of Ownable requires you to pass the initial owner to its constructor, as in the example. Always read the documentation for the exact version you install, and pin that version.

Check what you just learned

1. Why prefer OpenZeppelin to writing your own access control?
  • It is shorter only
  • It is widely reviewed, audited and battle-tested (correct)
  • It is free of risk
  • It runs off-chain

Reuse reduces the risk of new bugs.

Check what you just learned

1. OpenZeppelin v5's Ownable needs:
  • No constructor argument
  • A wallet
  • An initial owner passed to its constructor (correct)
  • A fee

Ownable(msg.sender).
keyPoints: Libraries share code without storage; OpenZeppelin provides audited building blocks.
Pin versions and read the documentation.

topics.title: Designing for reuse and safety
topics.html:
Principles
PrincipleWhy
Small, single-purpose contractsEasier to test and audit
Depend on interfaces, not implementationsSwap parts without rewriting
Prefer composition to deep inheritanceClarity
Use audited libraries for common featuresFewer bugs
Document who can do whatUsers and auditors need to know
Plan upgrades deliberatelyImmutable by default; upgrade only with strong governance
Worked example

A shape for a token vault

You want a vault that holds tokens and can be paused.

  1. Inherit Ownable for the owner.
  2. Inherit Pausable for the emergency stop.
  3. Use ReentrancyGuard on deposit and withdraw.
  4. Write only the vault's own logic yourself.

Answer. Most of the safety comes from reuse.

Common mistakes

  • Copying code from a forum without understanding it.
  • Mixing several incompatible library versions.
  • Inheriting from a contract whose internals you have not read.

Check what you just learned

1. Which approach usually gives the safest result?
  • Writing every feature yourself
  • Skipping tests
  • Copying unknown code
  • Reusing audited libraries for common features (correct)

Less new code, fewer new bugs.

Check what you just learned

1. A good reason to avoid deep inheritance is that:
  • It is hard to read and audit (correct)
  • It is illegal
  • It is cheap
  • It is fast

Complexity hides bugs.

Key terms: flip and sort

Inheritance
A contract reusing a parent's code
Interface
A declaration of functions only
Library
Reusable code without storage
override
Implements or replaces a parent function
OpenZeppelin
A widely used set of audited contract libraries
Composition
Building by combining parts
keyPoints: Small, composable, interface-driven designs with audited parts are safer.
Read and pin every dependency.

modules.title: Build a project: Crowdfund
modules.summary: A complete contract from specification to tests: pledges, deadlines, withdrawals and refunds.
modules.outcome: You can read a full contract, explain each rule, write tests for it and review it for bugs.
modules.intro: This last module brings everything together in one realistic project. You will read a full crowdfunding contract, understand the design, see how to test it and then review a flawed contract for bugs.

topics.title: The specification
topics.html:
Crowdfund is a contract in which a creator sets a funding goal and a deadline. Backers pledge ETH until the deadline. If the goal is met, the creator withdraws the money; if not, every backer can take their pledge back. Nobody has to trust the creator or the platform: the code enforces the rules.

The rules
RuleWhoWhen
Pledge any amountAnyoneBefore the deadline
Withdraw all fundsThe creator onlyAfter the deadline, if the goal was reached, once only
Refund a pledgeEach backerAfter the deadline, if the goal was not reached
Nothing else can move moneyNobodyAlways

Check what you just learned

1. When can a backer take a refund?
  • Any time
  • After the deadline if the goal was not reached (correct)
  • Only if the creator agrees
  • Never

The contract enforces it.

Check what you just learned

1. Who can withdraw the funds?
  • Anyone
  • Backers
  • Only the creator, after the deadline and only if the goal was reached (correct)
  • The owner at any time

Rules bind everyone.
keyPoints: Write the rules as who, what and when before coding.
The contract enforces the rules without trusting the creator.

topics.title: The code
topics.html:
Design choices to notice
ChoiceWhy
creator, goal and deadline are immutableCheap to read and impossible to change after deployment
pledged mapping records each backer's amountNeeded for refunds and for a fair history
Custom errors for every failureCheap and clear in wallets and tests
withdrawn flag set before sendingStops a second withdrawal and follows checks-effects-interactions
pledged[msg.sender] = 0 before sending a refundStops a repeated refund and blocks reentrancy
The call result is checked in both withdraw and refundA failing recipient reverts the whole action
Events for pledge, refund and withdrawApps can show live progress
Watch out

Even this tidy contract is for learning. A real campaign that holds other people's money should be tested far more, reviewed by others and audited before use.

Check what you just learned

1. Why is pledged[msg.sender] set to zero before the refund is sent?
  • To save gas
  • To emit an event
  • To change the owner
  • To prevent reentrancy and double refunds (correct)

State is updated before the external call.

Check what you just learned

1. The withdrawn flag stops:
  • A second withdrawal (correct)
  • Pledges
  • Events
  • Refunds

A one-time action.
keyPoints: Immutables, custom errors and checks-effects-interactions make the contract cheap and safe.
Every state change has a matching event.

topics.title: Testing and reviewing it
topics.html:
Tests turn the specification into checks. The following Hardhat test uses a helper to move the blockchain's clock forward, which lets us test behaviour that only happens after the deadline. Run it on your own computer after installing Node.js and Hardhat; the course platform does not run code.

Tests you should have
TestWhy
Pledge before the deadline works and emits an eventHappy path
Pledge after the deadline revertsDeadline rule
Withdraw before the deadline revertsTiming
Withdraw by a non-creator revertsAccess control
Withdraw with the goal missed revertsBusiness rule
Withdraw twice revertsOne-time action
Refund when the goal is reached revertsBusiness rule
Refund twice revertsDouble refund
A malicious recipient cannot re-enterSecurity

How to review a contract

  1. Read the specification first, then check that every rule appears in code.
  2. Look at every function that moves ETH: who can call it, and in what order does it act?
  3. Search for external calls and check what state is updated before them.
  4. Look for loops, assumptions about exact balances and dependence on block data.
  5. Ask what an attacker, a careless user and a hostile recipient could each do.

Check what you just learned

1. Why use time-manipulation helpers in tests?
  • To cheat
  • To test behaviour that depends on deadlines without waiting (correct)
  • To change the code
  • To lower gas

Tests need to move the clock.

Check what you just learned

1. A good review starts with:
  • The gas report
  • The logo
  • The specification (correct)
  • The price

Check the code against the intent.

Key terms: flip and sort

Specification
A written description of what a contract must do
Immutable
Set once at deployment
Test fixture
Reusable test setup
Time travel
Moving the test chain's clock
Invariant
A property that must always hold
Code review
Reading code for bugs against a specification
keyPoints: Test every rule, including the failing cases, and use time helpers for deadlines.
Review by reading the specification against the code, then thinking like an attacker.
